groups.text: A payments service reads events from Kafka as raw strings.
When each handler parses them itself, a bad amount fails in the ledger, after audit has already logged it.
This capstone builds one library that stops that.
Here it is, finished.
A raw record crosses one edge, and comes out as a typed event, or a rejection.
The bus runs its middleware, then the event's handlers.
Kotlin and Java code each get a door in.
Lesson one, in Kotlin, builds the model and the edge.
A sealed interface lists every event, so a when with no else must handle them all.
Ids and amounts are value classes, which check themselves when they're built.
And parseEvent turns raw fields into an event, or into Rejected.
It never throws.
Lesson two builds the bus.
It finds handlers by the event's class, then by each event supertype, nearest first.
A handler only takes events in, so Handler is declared in.
One audit handler fits every subscription.
Each subscription returns a handle, and one failing handler can't stop the others.
Logging and dropping duplicates run once per event, as a chain.
Timing one handler is a decorator around it.
Lesson three adds the A P I.
Kotlin code gets a subscription DSL.
It subscribes everything at once, when the block ends.
Its on function is reified, so it knows each event's class.
Java code gets Class overloads, and a facade that still builds the value classes, so every check runs.
The lab is Kotlin, plus one Java class that uses the library the way a Java team would.
One rule holds through all three lessons.
Raw fields are parsed once, at the edge.
Past that line, no handler reads a string, and every event is valid.
